name: Moor, Rieck, Horn, Jutzeler & Borgwardt (2021) 'Early Prediction of Sepsis in the ICU Using Machine Learning: A Systematic Review'. Used here as a methods analogue for event-onset forecasting: label definition, horizon, case-control onset matching, and label circularity (indirect-labelling leakage).
type: paper (systematic review, PRISMA) / method family (clinical event-onset prediction)
url: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2021.607952 ; PMC full text: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8193357/ ; medRxiv preprint (2020-08-31): https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.08.31.20185207 ; review data/code: https://github.com/BorgwardtLab/sepsis-prediction-review
year: 2021 (Frontiers in Medicine 8:607952, published 28 May 2021); medRxiv preprint Aug 2020
authors: Michael Moor, Bastian Rieck, Max Horn, Catherine R. Jutzeler, Karsten Borgwardt (ETH Zurich, D-BSSE; SIB Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics)
popularity: 239 citations on Semantic Scholar (queried 2026-10-17). The companion GitHub repo BorgwardtLab/sepsis-prediction-review has 5 stars, no license file, last push 2020-08-31.
peer_review_status: peer-reviewed (Frontiers in Medicine). It reviews 22 peer-reviewed studies; preprints and gray literature were excluded.
target_type: Onset. Every reviewed study predicts the START of sepsis, an event that is unobserved and is approximated by clinical criteria, within a horizon before onset. Patients already septic at or near admission are excluded from the cohort. That is the clinical analogue of our at-risk masking. The review notes that a state-like framing inflates scores. Example: Futoma et al. compared cases against controls at discharge (stable patients) and saw a 'drastic drop in performance' once that easy contrast was removed.
target_definition: Heterogeneous across studies. 12/22 (54.5%) used Sepsis-2-type definitions: SIRS plus suspected or confirmed infection, ICD-9 995.9 plus a 5-h persisting SIRS window, or SIRS plus a blood culture plus an abnormal vital sign. 9/22 (40.9%) used Sepsis-3: suspected infection (antibiotics plus culture) together with an acute SOFA increase of 2 or more within a 72-h window, from 48 h before to 24 h after suspected infection, often with modified windows. One study used clinician tags (daily labels only). One defined onset as the earliest of an antibiotic prescription or qSOFA criteria. Horizon H: 19/22 (86.4%) used 'offline training + horizon evaluation'. Predictions are made at fixed lead times before the (matched) onset, typically 0 to 4 h, with one 'next day' study. Some used one fixed 4-h horizon. 2/22 used online training and evaluation, which predicts at every hour and needs a choice of how many hours before or after onset count as positive. The PhysioNet 2019 challenge shifted labels to 6 h before onset. The review recommends always reporting H = 3 h or 4 h.
spatial_unit: Not spatial. The unit is the ICU patient stay (encounter), with hourly or irregular time stamps inside the stay.
at_risk_masking: Partly, through cohort exclusion rather than row masking. Studies removed patients whose onset falls too early: Moor et al. dropped onset within the first 7 h (the review notes this 'drastically reduced' the cohort), Nemati required onset at least 4 h after admission, Desautels kept onset between 7 and 500 h, and Schamoni and Sheetrit excluded onset before day 2 or day 3. Bloch and Calvert excluded patients meeting SIRS at admission. After onset, case time series are truncated at onset, so post-onset hours are never scored. This is equivalent to our rule 'rows already under alert at t are excluded'. The difference: an ICU stay has a single onset, whereas our units have recurrent events and need a recurring risk set.
data_sources: Literature search of Embase, Google Scholar, PubMed/Medline, Scopus and Web of Science. 974 records yielded 22 included studies (21 in the quality assessment). Underlying cohorts were mostly MIMIC-II/III, eICU, PhysioNet 2019 challenge data, and single-centre hospital EHRs (US/Europe). Only one non-Western cohort was included. Prevalence ranged from 3.3% to 63.6%, and 10/22 studies had 10% or less.
data_source_variant: Not applicable (no air-alert data). The analogue issue is that the same 'event' is labelled by different definitions (Sepsis-2 vs Sepsis-3 vs ICD codes vs clinician tags), and results are not comparable across definitions. Air alerts have the same problem across sources: official vs volunteer vs alerts.in.ua, oblast-only vs union of levels, and after Sep 2026 yellow vs red.
preprocessing: Typical pipeline in the reviewed studies: hourly binning or resampling of vitals and labs, forward filling or imputation (some use Gaussian-process imputation, as in Moor et al.'s MGP-TCN), cohort inclusion by age and length of stay, exclusion of early-onset cases, and truncation of case series at onset. Controls are assigned a pseudo-onset ('onset matching') and truncated there. Only 2/21 studies with computer-derived labels shared the label code, so the exact preprocessing is mostly not reproducible.
known_label_artefacts: 1) Onset time ambiguity: 'the exact sepsis onset is usually unknown', so onset is a proxy built from criteria with look-back windows (SOFA uses the worst values over the preceding 24 h; Sepsis-3 uses a 72-h window). The labelled onset time can therefore move relative to the true event. Analogue: an alert onset is an administrative announcement time, not the threat time, and sub-oblast alerts were merged into oblast intervals. 2) Indirect labelling / circularity: the label is computed from the same vitals and labs used as predictors, so classifiers 'may just confirm existing criteria'. The review argues it may be virtually impossible to separate label data from predictor data, and that even clinician tags carry indirect circularity. It notes no study had tested this empirically. 3) Control alignment: comparing cases against controls at discharge makes the task too easy. Random onset matching can create distributions that differ systematically, because onsets are not uniform over the stay. Moor et al. proposed absolute matching (same hours since admission) to avoid length-of-stay bias. 16/22 studies did not report how controls were matched. 4) Early-onset exclusion shrinks and biases the cohort. 5) Definition heterogeneity prevents meta-analysis. No alert-specific artefacts (duplicates, 30-min ends, standing alerts, recording gaps) apply.
model_family: Across the 22 studies: gradient-boosted trees (e.g., InSight / XGBoost-type), random forests, logistic and ElasticNet regression, SVMs, Weibull-Cox proportional hazards (Nemati's AISE), RNN/LSTM (e.g., SepLSTM), temporal convolutional networks with multitask Gaussian-process imputation (Moor et al. MGP-TCN), and others. The review does not rank model families, because heterogeneity precludes that.
features: Hourly vital signs (heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, SpO2), laboratory values (lactate, white cell count, creatinine, bilirubin, platelets, etc.), demographics, sometimes interventions and medications, plus derived trend and variability features (e.g., heart-rate variability, windowed statistics) and missingness indicators. Feature engineering was described in 81% of studies; predictor importance was explained in 38%. Spatial, calendar and external features are not applicable.
external_feature_timing: Not applicable (no ISW/Telegram-type external feeds). The related timing lesson: inputs such as antibiotic orders and culture draws are part of the Sepsis-3 suspected-infection definition. If they enter the feature set at or after the time they define the label, they leak the label. The review lists them only in label definitions and does not discuss them as predictor leakage [uncertain whether individual studies excluded them].
ablation_design: Not part of the review. Individual studies rarely ran controlled ablations on identical samples. The key comparison the review highlights, Futoma's discharge-matched vs relative-matched controls, is effectively an evaluation-design ablation: same model, different control alignment, with a large change in measured performance.
split_scheme: Mostly random patient-level splits or cross-validation inside one retrospective dataset. Only 3 studies validated on an external dataset (14% met the external-validation criterion). No prospective sepsis-onset validation was found; the only prospective study targeted mortality, length of stay and readmission. The review does not discuss time-based (walk-forward) splits [uncertain whether any included study used a temporal split].
metrics: AUROC in almost all studies. AUPRC in only 6. Sensitivity, specificity and PPV at chosen thresholds in some. The PhysioNet 2019 utility score (rewards early, penalises late or false alarms) for challenge-based studies. The review warns that AUROC 'depends on class prevalence', can look high when minority-class detection is poor, and recommends reporting prevalence and AUPRC.
unit_of_metric: Pooled over patient time points or prediction instances within each study. No within-unit averaging (each patient contributes one onset), and no cross-study pooling, because no meta-analysis was done.
baseline_strength: Weak. Most studies compared against clinical scores (SIRS, qSOFA, MEWS, SOFA) or other ML models, not against a strong naive forecaster. No climatology or recent-rate baseline exists in this literature. The review's main point is that weak or easy comparisons, especially discharge-time controls, overstate skill.
calibration: Not discussed in the review. Calibration of predicted probabilities is absent from the 14-item quality checklist, which is itself a gap.
calibration_under_drift: Not addressed directly. The review stresses external validation and geographic diversity, since only one non-Western cohort was included. The implicit concern is that performance and base rates shift between hospitals and over time, but no recalibration method is evaluated [uncertain].
uncertainty_of_gain: The review reports no CIs on skill differences. Stability or variance of results was reported by 62% of studies (a quality criterion). No study-level significance test on the gain over baselines is summarised.
regime_coverage: Not applicable to air alerts. The analogue is the definition change from Sepsis-2 to Sepsis-3 (2016), which split the literature into incomparable groups. This mirrors how the Sep-2026 yellow/red reform changes what an 'onset' is, so pre- and post-reform metrics should not be pooled (our D-015 and D-007).
leakage_handling: Discussed, or missed in the reviewed studies: 1) Label circularity: labels derived from features (SOFA from labs and vitals over 24-72 h windows) mean that data used to label onset overlap the data used to predict it. Within a horizon of a few hours, the inputs may already contain the label-defining abnormalities, so 'prediction' partly re-detects the criteria. Untested empirically in the literature. 2) Control alignment as hidden leakage: discharge-time controls encode 'patient is stable and leaving', information unavailable at a matched real-time point. Random matching can encode length-of-stay differences, and absolute matching is recommended. 3) Truncation at onset: case inputs must stop at the prediction time before onset, i.e. horizon evaluation. The review notes that predicting closer to onset is progressively easier, so reporting only H = 0 inflates skill. 4) Code to reproduce labels was released by only 2 studies, so leakage cannot be audited. Not covered: purging across temporal cut-offs, truncation tests, and causal feature audits.
test_window_hygiene: Not systematically reported. Hyperparameters were reported in only 29% of studies, platforms in 19%, analysis code in 10% and label code in 10%, so it is usually unknowable how often test sets were consulted. No pre-registration was reported. The review cites probable publication bias (no negative results).
headline_results: 22 studies were included. Quality ranged from 36% to 93% of 14 criteria; Kaji et al. and Moor et al. were best at 93%, and none met all criteria. Reported AUROC in early-prediction setups ranged from 0.78 (Shashikumar, ElasticNet, 4 h) to 0.99 (Kam and Kim, SepLSTM, 0 h, only 360 encounters). Massive heterogeneity in sepsis definition, horizon, onset matching and outcomes precluded meta-analysis. 72.7% of studies gave no onset-matching details. Only 2 shared code and only 4 reported on public data. Whether the models beat naive baselines is generally unknown, since no strong naive forecaster was used.
code_available: Review data (study extraction tables) at https://github.com/BorgwardtLab/sepsis-prediction-review (5 stars, no license file, inactive since Aug 2020). Of the reviewed studies, only Kaji et al. and Moor et al. released analysis and label code (Moor et al.'s MGP-TCN code is in the BorgwardtLab GitHub) [uncertain on exact repo name].
takeaways_for_project: 1) Our at-risk masking (target rule; assert test) is the analogue of truncating case series at onset and excluding already-septic patients. Cite this as standard practice: scoring rows under alert would turn onset forecasting into state detection and inflate AUC, just as discharge-matched controls inflated sepsis scores (Futoma's 'drastic drop'). 2) Indirect-labelling leakage maps to our label-defining data: the onset label and features like active_at_t, minutes_since_last_end and neighbors_active are built from the same alert intervals. That is fine only if every feature uses data with timestamp <= t and the label uses (t, t+H]. The hidden analogue is the D-020 standing-alert rule: classifying an alert as standing via its final finished_at would be the same circularity (label logic reading the future). Keep the causal 24h cap and the negative-control leaky feature in tests/test_leakage.py. 3) Horizon reporting: performance gets easier closer to onset, so H must be fixed and stated (default H = 1). If H is varied, report all values rather than the best. Sepsis papers that reported only H = 0 looked best. 4) Control alignment maps to row sampling: we score ALL unmasked hourly rows (no sampling of negatives). That avoids the random or discharge-matching biases the review criticises. Do not subsample negatives for evaluation, and if negatives are downsampled for training, re-weight or recalibrate. 5) Prevalence and PR-AUC: the review's recommendation to report prevalence and AUPRC alongside AUROC matches our D-rule (PR-AUC and PR-AUC / base rate; print base rates at each stage). Report the base rate per group (Kyiv City / frontline / rear), since rear oblasts are rare-event. 6) Strong baselines: the sepsis literature's weakness is comparing against clinical scores only. Our rolling recent-rate baseline as primary BSS reference (D-021) is exactly the strong naive baseline that literature lacks. Say so in the README. 7) Definition changes: the Sepsis-2 to Sepsis-3 split shows that a target-definition change breaks comparability. That supports keeping the official and API (yellow/red) sources apart (D-007, D-015) and stating the onset definition (union of levels, D-020) precisely, with code. 8) Reproducibility checklist: release the label code (grid.py and the target builder), hyperparameters, package versions (pinned requirements.txt) and data-access instructions. These are criteria that 80-90% of sepsis studies failed. 9) Early-in-series exclusion: like dropping onset in the first 7 h of a stay, the first days after the 2022-03-23 series start and after the 2026-08-30 to 09-01 recording gap have unknown history. Mask or flag them (D-013) rather than treating them as 'no prior alert'. 10) Calibration is missing from the sepsis checklist; our required reliability plot (D-006) and calibration-in-the-large check go beyond that literature.
best_practices: Adopt: (a) define the onset label in code and publish it; (b) state the horizon explicitly and report a fixed, pre-declared H (the review asks for 3-4 h; ours is 1 h); (c) exclude units already in the event state at prediction time (risk set) and truncate inputs at prediction time; (d) report prevalence plus AUPRC alongside AUROC; (e) describe exactly how negatives are formed, preferring full-population scoring or absolute alignment over random or end-of-stay matching; (f) validate externally or out of time (for us: walk-forward and the exploratory new-regime check); (g) publish hyperparameters, package versions and code; (h) explicitly discuss label circularity and test for it (our truncation test with a negative control is a direct empirical answer to the review's 'untested' gap). Avoid: (i) easy negatives (stable or discharge-time controls; for us, scoring rows under alert or quiet nights only); (ii) reporting only the easiest horizon; (iii) AUROC alone on rare events; (iv) labels computed with look-back or look-ahead windows that overlap the forecast origin without an audit; (v) comparing models only against weak rule-based scores; (vi) pooling results across different event definitions (Sepsis-2/3; for us official vs yellow/red); (vii) unreported test-set usage and no released code.
